Circle Through Incenter

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch the circle through two corners and the middle of its angle bisectors.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the clues and press Reset triangle to start again.
Look for the math

Draw a circle through two corners of a triangle and through the point where its three angle bisectors meet. Wherever you drag the corners, the circle slices equal lengths off the two sides that meet at the third corner.

The circle and its middle

The point I is the incenter: it is the same distance from all three sides, because it lies on every angle bisector. The circle through A, B and I is just the circumcircle of those three points. Its centre O turns out to lie on the bisector from C: turn on Show hint to see that line pass straight through the middle of the circle. The logic test checks this on more than three hundred triangles, and it holds every time.

Two equal cuts

Let X be the second point where the circle meets the line AC, and Y the second point where it meets BC. The claim is AX = BY. It comes from an angle count: writing half the angles of the triangle as α, β, γ, the angle AIB is 90° + γ, and the arcs cut off by the two chords then work out equal. Equal arcs give equal chords, and so AX = BY. Show premises marks those angles; Show statement marks the two matching lengths. The test compares the applet's own circle-and-line calculation with the page's formula on every triangle and finds the lengths agree.

The applet's original problem puts X on AC and Y on BC. The later summary page swaps those two letters; the applet and the original problem agree with this page. The condition AC ≠ BC in the problem is a red herring: when the two sides are equal, X is simply A and Y is B, so both lengths are zero.

More places the centre goes

The centre of (ABI) also sits on the circumcircle of ABC, another fact the test confirms on every configuration. The circle itself is symmetric about the bisector from C, because its centre lies on that line. The second crossing J of the circle with the bisector is the point used in the angle count; Show hint draws it.

A chord as long as AB

There is a point E on the circle with BE = AB. For that point, angle ABE = angle ACB, and the chord BE is perpendicular to the line from B to the circumcenter of ABC. The applet mentions both properties on its summary page; the logic test checks them by constructing E and measuring, rather than taking the statement on trust.

Try a long, thin triangle: the circle may leave the picture, but the two coloured cuts stay the same length.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
